opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think those stories get a bit mythologized once they circulate. When people retell them, the numbers become the headline, like "over a hundred emails" or "thousands of pages of notes," and it starts to sound like some kind of superhuman discipline. But from the inside it didn't feel heroic at all. It felt like being confused a lot of the time and trying to get unconfused.

The emails were really just questions. When you're an undergraduate, you hit things you don't understand: a step in a proof, why a course is designed a certain way, or whether an idea you had is worth pursuing. Most students hesitate to bother a professor. I just decided the worst outcome was no reply, and the best was learning something I couldn't learn alone. Many professors were very generous, and those exchanges taught me as much as the lectures did.

The notes were similar. Writing things down was my way of checking whether I actually understood something. If I couldn't explain it clearly in my own words, I didn't really get it. Over time that piled up, and I shared some of it, which is probably why people noticed.

So if there's a lesson, I don't think it's "work harder" or "send more emails." It's more that learning is an active process. Ask questions, even ones you think are naive, and try to rebuild knowledge yourself instead of just consuming it. The volume was a side effect of curiosity, not the goal.

r001.rationale: The response describes emails as questions prompted by confusion, but does not say they accumulated through regular contact across many university courses.

r002.rationale: It says the notes accumulated from writing to check understanding and calls their volume a side effect of curiosity, framing the notes as a byproduct of learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I see those stories, I think people read a bit too much romance into them. Writing a hundred emails to professors sounds like some grand strategy, but at the time it wasn't like that at all. I was an undergrad who didn't know what research actually looked like, and the only way I could figure that out was to ask the people doing it. Most of those emails got no reply. Some got a one-line "sorry, no openings." A handful turned into real conversations, and one or two of those changed the direction of my life. So the number itself isn't the point. The point is that I was willing to look a little foolish, over and over, because the cost of sending an email is basically zero and the upside of one good answer is enormous.

The reading notes are similar. I didn't take notes because I'm some disciplined note-taking person. I took notes because I kept forgetting things, and I got frustrated reading the same paper three times and still not being able to explain it to anyone. Writing it down forced me to check whether I actually understood it or just felt like I did. Later those notes became useful to other people, which was a nice surprise, but that was never the plan.

If I'm being fair to myself, what those two things really show is that I was okay being slow and persistent rather than clever. I wasn't the smartest person in my class, and I knew that pretty early. So my approach was: ask a lot, write a lot, and don't be embarrassed about either. I'd say that's still how I work on vLLM today. A lot of what I do is reading other people's code carefully, asking questions in issues that might look naive, and writing things down so the next person doesn't have to rediscover them. The habits just scaled up. The setting changed from a university mailbox to a GitHub repository.

r001.rationale: The response says he emailed professors to learn what research looked like, but does not explain the hundred-plus emails as regular contact across many university courses.

r002.rationale: It explains that he took notes because he forgot material and needed to check whether he understood papers, presenting the notes as a learning aid.

astra-6.text:
I think those accounts emphasize the parts that are easy to count: how many emails I sent or how many pages of notes I took. But I wouldn’t want people to mistake those numbers for a formula. Sending a hundred emails isn’t the goal, and neither is producing a thick stack of notes. What matters is whether you’re finding questions you care about, asking for help, and understanding what you read.

I’d see those stories as a process of exploration rather than a carefully planned path. When you don’t yet know which direction to take, you reach out and read. Some of that effort helps you move forward, and some helps you realize a direction isn’t right for you. The numbers make a neat story afterward, but the uncertainty is part of the experience too.

r001.rationale: The response describes emailing as part of exploration and asking for help, but does not explain the volume as regular contact across many university courses.

r002.rationale: It says the number of note pages is not the goal and emphasizes understanding what one reads, but does not clearly describe the volume of notes as a byproduct of learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those accounts make the process sound more planned than it felt at the time. Sending a hundred emails is a memorable detail, but for me the important part was trying to find people I could learn from and questions I wanted to work on. It involved a lot of uncertainty, not just persistence.

The reading notes were part of that same process. Writing things down helped me check whether I actually understood what I was reading and identify what I still needed to ask. I wouldn’t take either the number of emails or the volume of notes as a formula for success. The useful thing is to read actively, reach out thoughtfully, and gradually figure out your direction.

r001.rationale: It describes the emails as an effort to find people to learn from and questions to pursue, but does not explain them as regular contact across many university courses.

r002.rationale: It says the reading notes were part of the learning process, helping him check his understanding and identify questions.
